examples.label: See which account the instance runs as

notes:
=== MSSQL Instance Discovery ===
Enumerate SQL Server instances before attempting authentication or exploitation.

=== DISCOVERY METHODS ===
Network scan:
  nmap -p 1433,1434 --script ms-sql-info,ms-sql-empty-password <TARGET>
  UDP 1434 (SQL Browser): nmap -sU -p 1434 --script ms-sql-info <TARGET>

Local enumeration (on compromised Windows host):
  Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Name -like 'MSSQL*'}
  reg query "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Microsoft SQL Server\Instance Names\SQL"
  netstat -ano | findstr 1433

Snaffler for credential files:
  .\Snaffler.exe -s -d <domain> -o snaffler.log -v data
  Finds: web.config, *.config, appsettings.json, *.sql, connections.ini

=== INSTANCE NAMING ===
Default instance: SERVER (port 1433)
Named instance: SERVER\INSTANCENAME (dynamic port, SQL Browser on 1434 reveals it)
Always check both default and named instances via nmap + SQL Browser

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
Discovery → credentials from share → mssqlclient.py → xp_cmdshell → SeImpersonate → SYSTEM
Multiple MSSQL instances → linked servers across instances → lateral movement through SQL
MSSQL on DC → highest value target (machine account has DC-level access in some configs)

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
MSSQL running on Domain Controllers (rare but extremely high-value)
SA account with blank or weak password
Windows-authenticated users with sysadmin role
SQL Agent service account with sysadmin → agent job execution = RCE as that service account

recommended.note: Enable command exec on the discovered instance.

name: MSSQL - Discover Instance & Service Account
description: Locate installed SQL Server instances and identify the account each service runs as. If the service account holds SeImpersonatePrivilege it is the pivot for a potato attack.

defense.why_it_works: sc query / wmic service discovery reveals running SQL Server instances and, critically, the service account they run under. If the service account is highly privileged (Local System, Domain Admin, a misconfigured service account), compromising MSSQL credentials leads directly to system or domain admin access. Instance discovery is the reconnaissance step enabling targeted SQL attacks.
defense.prerequisites: Shell access. WMI query rights (standard user can query Win32_Service). Knowledge of MSSQL client tools.
defense.impact: Identifies SQL Server instances and their service account context. Enables targeted attack planning: if MSSQL runs as Local System, xp_cmdshell provides SYSTEM access.
defense.detection: sc query containing 'SQL' executed by standard user. WMI Win32_Service query filtered for SQL. net start output analyzed for SQL services.
defense.artifacts: Process log: sc query / wmic service query by standard user | SIEM: SQL service enumeration pattern
defense.prevention: Run SQL Server as a dedicated low-privilege service account with only the permissions needed for MSSQL operation. Document all SQL instances. Monitor for SQL service enumeration in SIEM.
defense.misconfiguration: SQL Server running as NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM or a domain admin account. Multiple SQL instances not inventoried. No service account least-privilege review.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Enumerate SQL instances:
sc query type= all | findstr SQL
wmic service where 'name like "%sql%"' get Name,StartName
# Output: MSSQL$SQLEXPRESS StartName: LocalSystem <- misconfigured
defense.secure_config:
# Correct service account setup:
# Create dedicated MSSQL service account:
New-ADUser -Name svc_mssql -Enabled $true -PasswordNeverExpires $true

# Assign minimal rights in SQL:
CREATE LOGIN [INLANEFREIGHT\svc_mssql] FROM WINDOWS;
EXEC sp_addsrvrolemember 'INLANEFREIGHT\svc_mssql', 'public'; -- no sysadmin

# Verify service account:
wmic service where 'name="MSSQL$SQLEXPRESS"' get StartName
defense.evasion: Pick the potato that matches the OS (GodPotato for 2019/2022) to avoid crashes and alerts; run it in-memory; the SeImpersonate abuse itself is quiet — the noisy part is the spawned shell, so route it through an existing C2 channel.
